narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 72.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Being in the bottom decile of your class, compared to an average of roughly the middle of the class among accepted students, signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure. At 25.5, it sits well below the average of 37.2 among students who were admitted, indicating the model saw this as another substantial risk for not passing on the first try.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted risk of failure. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model viewed this as a mild positive but not enough to overcome the other signals.

Your first-year class rank, family income bracket, and plan to attend full-time had smaller effects and did not change the overall picture.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic preparation and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Many students successfully reapply after addressing these specific gaps.
